query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy coatings operating at high temperature, a refined grain structure (achieved via a rapid quench after deposition) increases the density of grain boundaries and promotes thermally activated dislocation cross‐slip. This mechanism enhances dynamic recovery and distributes plastic deformation more uniformly under sliding loads, thereby reducing localized stress concentrations and yielding improved wear resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy coating produced by standard processing (e.g., conventional laser cladding) that exhibits a relatively coarse grain structure.
generation.intervention: Apply a rapid quenching process post-deposition to refine the grain structure relative to the baseline condition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding (e.g., 500–600 °C) against a conventional metal substrate, where thermal activation enables enhanced dislocation mobility and cross‐slip.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased grain boundary density and a modified dislocation substructure that facilitate cross‐slip.
generation.mechanism: Grain refinement creates more grain boundaries that act as effective sources for dislocations and promote cross‐slip under high-temperature conditions. This enhanced dislocation cross‐slip facilitates dynamic recovery, distributes deformation more evenly, and reduces the intensity of localized plastic flow, which otherwise would lead to increased wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline coating, the quenched (grain-refined) coating will exhibit lower wear rates and a more uniform, less localized deformation pattern during high-temperature sliding tests.
generation.baseline: The baseline condition is the as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating with larger, coarser grains showing more localized plastic deformation and higher wear rates under sliding in the high-temperature regime.
generation.boundary: These improvements are expected to be significant in the high-temperature regime where thermally activated dislocation processes (including cross-slip) are operative. At lower temperatures, the effect may be diminished or not observable.
generation.uncertainty: While the role of grain refinement in promoting cross-slip is supported in similar high-temperature alloy systems, the exact quantitative impact on wear resistance in this specific FeNiCrCoCu HEA remains uncertain. Effects of other factors such as potential phase changes or oxidation at high temperatures need further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings with identical compositions: one set processed by the standard (slow-cooling) method, and a second set subjected to rapid quenching to induce grain refinement. Conduct high-temperature sliding tests (e.g., pin-on-disk tests at 500–600 °C) on both sets. Characterize and compare the wear tracks, wear rates, and microstructural features using SEM, TEM (for dislocation configurations, cross-slip evidence) and measure friction coefficients.
measurements: Grain size and grain boundary density (via SEM/TEM)
Wear rate (measured as volume or weight loss)
Dislocation arrangements and evidence of enhanced cross-slip (TEM images)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid quenching does not lead to a statistically significant reduction in wear rate or fails to show evidence of increased dislocation cross-slip and more homogeneous plastic deformation compared to the baseline sample, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Effect of Alloying Elements on the High-Temperature Yielding Behavior of Multicomponent γ′-L12 Alloys

Abstract: The exceptional mechanical properties of Ni-based high entropy alloys are due to the presence of ordered L12 (γ′) precipitates embedded within a disordered matrix phase. While the strengthening contribution of the γ′ phase is generally accepted, there is no consensus on the precise contribution of the individual strengthening mechanisms to the overall strength. In addition, changes in alloy composition influence several different mechanisms, making the assessment of alloying conditions complex. Multicomponent L12-ordered single-phase alloys were systematically developed with the aid of CALPHAD thermodynamic calculations. The alloying elements Co, Cr, Ti, and Nb were chosen to complexify the Ni3Al structure. The existence of the γ′ single phase was validated by microstructure characterization and phase identification. Wear and Corrosion Resistance of Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Coating Deposited on AZ91D Magnesium Alloy by Laser Cladding

Abstract: AbstractIn order to improve the wear and corrosion resistance of an AZ91D magnesium alloy substrate, an Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy coating was successfully prepared on an AZ91D magnesium alloy surface by laser cladding using mixed elemental powders. Optical microscopy (OM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and X-ray diffraction were used to characterize the microstructure of the coating. The wear resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating were evaluated by dry sliding wear and potentiodynamic polarization curve test methods, respectively. The results show that the coating was composed of a simple FCC solid solution phase with a microhardness about 3.7 times higher than that of the AZ91D matrix and even higher than that of the same high-entropy alloy prepared by an arc melting method. The coating had better wear resistance than the AZ91D matrix, and the wear rate was about 2.5 times lower than that of the AZ91D matrix.
